register.name: Indiana General Assembly - Indiana Code (published by the Legislative Services Agency)
register.access_notes: Verified, but only through the site's own client-side rendering. iga.in.gov is a React single-page app: a plain HTTPS client with an honest user agent gets the same 691-byte app shell for every path, including /laws/current/ic/titles/22 and the static data paths. The documented API host api.iga.in.gov answers without a key with HTTP 403 and the body {'error': '403', 'message': 'x-api-key not found'} - no key was requested, guessed or used, and nothing was worked around. Instead the site's own pages were rendered in a real browser with JavaScript enabled (an honest browser, not a spoofed user agent), and that is where the Code data was read: the app itself requests same-origin static files at https://iga.in.gov/ic/2026/Title_<n>.json, each entry carrying type, number, name, year and a public flag, and those files were read in the page context. Currency: the human path https://iga.in.gov/laws/current/ic redirects to https://iga.in.gov/laws/2026/ic/titles/1, and every entry read carried year '2026' and public true, so 'current' is the 2026 edition of the Indiana Code. About 20 requests in all (2 plain-HTTP probes, 1 API probe, browser navigations, and 12 in-page data fetches spaced 1.8 seconds apart). No CAPTCHA, no rate limiting and no bot challenge was encountered on iga.in.gov. Separately, https://www.in.gov/core/policies.html (the statewide terms page) was unreachable from this environment ('connect ECONNREFUSED 208.40.244.65:443'), so the statewide policy text could not be read.

licence.summary: No copyright notice, licence or terms-of-use statement appears anywhere on the register: the footer of iga.in.gov ends with the Statehouse address and no copyright line, and a scan of the site's FAQ page for the words copyright, reproduce, public domain and terms of use returned nothing. The statute text is therefore unencumbered on its own terms, and under the government edicts doctrine (Georgia v. Public.Resource.Org, 590 U.S. 255 (2020)) the text of the Indiana Code is not copyrightable at all: reuse and adaptation are permissible. Two cautions. First, the statewide State of Indiana terms page at www.in.gov could not be read from this environment, so a state-portal-level assertion cannot be ruled out. Second, the official Indiana Code is compiled by the Legislative Services Agency, while the annotated editions (Burns Indiana Statutes Annotated from LexisNexis, and West's Annotated Indiana Code) are commercial products whose annotations and editorial matter are protected - only the bare Code as published on iga.in.gov should be taken.

register.name: Kansas Statutes on the Kansas Legislature's site (statutes compiled by the Office of Revisor of Statutes)
register.access_notes: BLOCK ENCOUNTERED AND RESPECTED, then an official alternative used. The Revisor's own site, https://www.ksrevisor.gov/, answers HTTP 200 but returns a bot-verification interstitial instead of content: the body of both https://www.ksrevisor.gov/statutes/ and the section page https://www.ksrevisor.gov/statutes/chapters/ch44/044_003_0013.html was only 'One moment, please... Loader Please wait while your request is being verified...' with no statute text and no real links. That challenge was NOT solved, bypassed or retried in a loop - two requests, then stop. Verification was done instead on the Kansas Legislature's own site, which publishes the same Revisor-compiled statutes as plain server-rendered HTML and served every request with HTTP 200 and no challenge. URL shapes used: chapter index https://www.kslegislature.gov/li/b2025_26/statute/<ccc>_000_0000_chapter/ (lists the articles with their names) and article page https://www.kslegislature.gov/li/b2025_26/statute/<ccc>_000_0000_chapter/<ccc>_<aaa>_0000_article/ (lists every section number and catchline). Currency: every page carries the heading '2026 Kansas Statutes'. About 17 requests in total, all with an honest user agent (canon-index-builder/1.0) and spaced 2 seconds apart. licence.summary: Kansas does assert copyright, unusually plainly for a US register: every statute page ends with a Revisor notice and the site footer claims all rights reserved, and the Kansas.gov portal policies claim the compilation of site content as the property of the Information Network of Kansas. Those assertions cannot reach the statute text itself: under the government edicts doctrine (Georgia v. Public.Resource.Org, 590 U.S. 255 (2020)) work an official produces in the course of official duties - including a state's statutes - is not copyrightable, so the text of the Kansas Statutes is free to reuse and adapt. What the assertions can plausibly cover is the compilation, arrangement and any editorial matter, i.e. the selection and ordering of the site's pages rather than the enacted words. Practical consequence: take the statutory text, do not mirror the site's own compilation wholesale, and expect no permission problem for an adapted encoding. The official Kansas Statutes Annotated is compiled by the Office of Revisor of Statutes (a legislative agency, not a commercial publisher), though the annotated print edition is distributed commercially.

topic_gaps.reason: No Kansas statute grants leave or holiday pay. Private-sector vacation, sick and holiday pay is a matter of contract or policy, enforceable only as wages under K.S.A. ch. 44, art. 3. For state employees, leave is set by regulation (K.A.R. art. 1-9) under the Kansas Civil Service Act, K.S.A. ch. 75, art. 29, whose only statutory leave hook is 75-2947 'Transfers; leaves of absence; reinstatements.' (verified on the register's 2026 article listing); K.S.A. 75-3707, which is sometimes cited for this, is in fact 'Functions of department in general.' and grants no leave. Chapter 35 'HOLIDAYS AND DAYS OF COMMEMORATION' (seen on the register's chapter index) only designates days and confers no pay entitlement. Family and medical leave is federal (FMLA, 29 U.S.C. 2601).
